Major technology corporations are approaching maximum borrowing boundaries within the global bond sector, Wells Fargo warns.

Market participants are penalizing individual debt offerings that surpass $25 billion.

Combined issuance from top hyperscalers, alongside data center developments by firms like Nvidia and SpaceX, has driven total volume to roughly $400 billion for the year.

The massive financial push by hyperscalers, cloud architecture firms, and data center operators to build AI infrastructure has hit structural limits in international debt markets, according to Wells Fargo.

Maureen O'Connor, global head of high-grade debt syndicate at Wells Fargo, characterized the recent trend as a distinct "supply shock" affecting the $15 trillion investment-grade landscape. Speaking on Bloomberg TV, O'Connor emphasized that the market is rapidly nearing its saturation ceiling.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

Surging Corporate Bond Volumes

Primary tech hyperscalers like Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, Meta, and Oracle have collectively brought over $200 billion in corporate bonds to market within the current calendar year. When factoring in specialized data center funding initiatives from industry players like Nvidia Corp. and SpaceX, aggregate volume surges to approximately $400 billion, Wells Fargo noted.

According to O'Connor, bond offerings that eclipse the $25 billion threshold are now facing negative reactions in secondary trading. Consequently, financial advisors recommend that individual issuers limit their visits to the bond market to twice a year.

"We have definitely recognized a bit of a pivot point in and around about $25 billion per issuance being a bit of a pain point for investors," O'Connor stated during the broadcast. "It puts a little bit of a lid on how much these companies can actually borrow directly from the investment-grade market."

Looking ahead, O'Connor anticipates a structural shift in how firms secure capital for AI hardware components, projecting expanded use of off-balance-sheet financing models next year, specifically tailored for graphics processing units (GPUs) and tensor processing units (TPUs).

AMZN, GOOGL, MSFT Stock: Retail View

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was 'bearish' towards Amazon stock and was 'neutral' for Microsoft and Alphabet stock, with 'normal' to 'high' message volumes.

AMZN stock has gained 15%, Microsoft has added 8%, and Google has lost 4% year-to-date.

CIBC Capital Markets recommended a list of top stock picks after the Democratic sweep of Congress, according to CNBC, citing a potentially tougher regulatory environment for corporate America. In a report published the day after the midterm vote, the Canadian bank said its Democratic basket was designed to hold up in a more defensive market, driven by a less business-friendly environment. It had built two baskets before the election: one for a Democratic-controlled Congress and one for a Republican-controlled Congress.

The Democratic list holds 36 stocks. The bank leaned toward major technology platforms and multinational companies over domestic ones, and it tilted toward lower-volatility names wherever it could, expecting investors to grow more cautious. The basket also stretches across consumer staples, real estate, health care, financials and utilities, so it is not only a technology bet. Beyond the largest technology companies, it also picked businesses in cybersecurity, consulting, payments, health insurance, waste services and utilities.

How CIBC Reads a Regulation-Driven Market

Christopher Harvey, CIBC's head of equity and portfolio strategy, wrote that in a more regulation-driven scenario, the bank would trim its exposure to the suppliers that build out AI infrastructure and lean toward the large cloud platforms and software companies.

The Republican basket is the mirror image. Its 45 names favor AI exposure, based on expectations of limited regulation and less resistance to data-center construction under a Republican-led Senate. Together, the two lists work as opposing bets on how much Washington will push back on corporate America. Readers following the group can find more names in our list of tech stocks investors are talking about.

Why Data Centers May Still Get Built

Harvey also cautioned against writing off the data center boom. Campaign promises should be respected, he wrote, but data centers bring jobs, economic growth and a larger tax base that most politicians want, and few of them want the blame for losing the AI race to China. CNBC separately reported that some economists see political pushback as a way to let some air out of an AI bubble without popping it. For another set of names, see our ranking of the most promising technology stocks to buy right now.

Not every group rallied on the news. Defense stocks slid more than 2% on Wednesday on fears that Democrats will curb spending, although Wolfe Research analyst Myles Walton told clients the knee-jerk reaction could fade quickly, pointing to past cases in which defense contractors recovered from election-driven sell-offs. Overall, the Dow had soared 1,500 points that day, its best session since April 2025.

Watching Snap (SNAP) stock lose 18.2% since its October 12 close likely leaves you asking whether this is a chance to buy or the start of a longer slide. The bulk of that drop hit on November 5, when shares lost 14.0% the day after Snap's third-quarter report missed expectations on revenue and daily active users. This fall, at 18.2%, is smaller than the 20% falls in Snap's record. So how far have Snap shares climbed after those deeper falls?

How Far Has Snap Stock Climbed After Past Falls?

At their best, Snap shares climbed a median 43.8% within a year of a past fall, but a year later the typical fall had erased all of that climb and more. Snap has had 20 falls of more than 20% since March 2, 2017, and 18 of them now have a full year behind them. Only 5 of those 18 left the shares higher twelve months on, and the median result was a loss of 22.0%. The other two falls, in February and June 2026, are too recent to judge.

It also took patience and nerve to reach those best prices. The median best price arrived 128 days, or about four months, after the fall. During the year after a drop, the lowest close sat a median 43.6% below the price on the day of the fall. Year-later results ranged from a loss of 85.0% to a gain of 371.0%, landing far from the median in both directions.

Amazon Stocks Gain as Anthropic IPO Puts $271.8 Billion Value on Stake
Khac Phu Nguyen

ANTH.PVT
Trade AMZN on Coinbase

This article first appeared on GuruFocus.

Amazon.com Inc (NASDAQ:AMZN) shares gained 1.08% to $269.05 at 9:35 a.m. ET in early regular-session trading on November 12 as investors priced Amazon's position in Anthropic ahead of next week's IPO. Reuters valued the stake at about $271.8 billion at $78 a share against $18.0 billion invested, according to CoinCentral.

Warning! GuruFocus has detected 6 Warning Signs with AMZN.

Is AMZN fairly valued? Test your thesis with our free DCF calculator.

AMZN GF Value chart

The structure matters. Amazon faces a 12% ownership cap under its notes, so its shares arrive in stages: it will hold 1,920,511,218 Class N shares after the offering, with 1,563,617,444 more to be issued later, CoinCentral reported. Anthropic's amended S-1 sets an 825 million-share offering at $70 to $78 and shows revenue of $17.0 billion for the three months ended September 30, 2026. Holders of more than 0.5% of fully diluted shares face lock-ups of up to 365 days.

At $271.8 billion, the stake equals about 9.3% of Amazon's $2.91 trillion market value, a meaningful hidden asset that turns visible next week. It is still paper value: long lock-ups and staged issuance mean Amazon cannot realize it quickly, and mark-to-market swings could add volatility to reported earnings. GuruFocus gives Amazon a GF Score of 94/100, with an 8/10 profitability rank and 7/10 financial strength. At $269.05, the shares sit 3.9% above the GF Value of $259.07, a "Fairly Valued" reading, at about 21.8 times earnings. The test is the November 18 pricing and whether AWS keeps winning Anthropic's compute spending after the listing.

title: Warren Buffett's Successor, Greg Abel, Has Nearly $110 Billion Invested in These 2 Tech Stocks

Warren Buffett's Successor, Greg Abel, Has Nearly $110 Billion Invested in These 2 Tech Stocks

Since Greg Abel took over the reins at Berkshire Hathaway (NYSE: BRKA)(NYSE: BRKB) after longtime CEO Warren Buffett retired at the end of last year, the company has made notable portfolio changes. It got rid of stakes in blue chips like Amazon and UnitedHealth Group, but kept Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) as its top holding and turned its stake in Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG)(NASDAQ: GOOGL) up a notch.

As of June 30, Berkshire owns 227,917,808 Apple shares, worth around $79.4 billion at its Nov. 10 share price. It also owns 105,979,600 shares of Alphabet (both share classes), worth around $30.4 billion. Together, they make up over 30% of Berkshire's stock portfolio.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Given Berkshire's investing record and its bullish stance on both companies, should investors follow suit? I believe so.

Image source: The Motley Fool.
Apple is picking up steam again

Berkshire started selling a lot of its Apple shares in 2024 and 2025, dropping from around 915 million shares at its mid-2023 peak to nearly 228 million today. Berkshire hasn't bought or sold Apple shares since Abel took over, so it seems Abel is comfortable holding steady.

So far this year, not selling definitely seems like the smart route because Apple's stock is thriving. Through Nov. 10, it's up over 28%, leading all "Magnificent Seven" stocks by a nice margin. It's also up 7% since John Ternus replaced longtime CEO Tim Cook on Sept. 1.

Part of the reason Apple's stock has been thriving is that investors are shying away from some major tech stocks that are spending aggressively on AI and are embracing the stability and predictability that come with Apple. During the earlier phases of the current AI boom, Apple got a lot of flak for seemingly lagging in the arms race. Now, its discipline is paying off.

Apple's revenue growth has been unimpressive leading up to this year, but it has accelerated a bit. In its fiscal 2026 (ended Sept. 26), the company generated $478.8 billion in revenue, up 15% year over year, and increased its earnings per share (EPS) by 20% to $8.98.

AAPL Revenue (Annual YoY Growth) data by YCharts

Apple noted that it sold the most iPhones in company history in its September-ended quarter, an encouraging sign that the company still has momentum with its main moneymaker.

Its stronghold on consumer hardware should remain strong. It won't have the revenue and earnings growth you're seeing from companies like Nvidia and other AI standouts. Still, I expect it to continue delivering good long-term returns.
